t: The eye of humankind, or the cities of Aram?
p: The Hebrew says 'the eye of humankind'; the Greek has the LORD watching people; a modern guess changes the letters to 'cities of Aram.'

readings.w: A conjecture of some modern commentators (not attributed to one here)

why: The Hebrew is read two ways without any change (people look to the LORD, or the LORD watches people; see the note). The conjecture takes the phrase as a place name in the list of Syrian cities and has no manuscript behind it. The Plain follows the first sense of the Hebrew; the Greek 'Sedrach' for Hadrach in the same verse shows how hard the line was.

t: A sea of distress, or a narrow sea?
p: The Hebrew says 'sea of trouble'; the Greek has 'narrow sea,' which recalls the Sea of Reeds.
why: The Hebrew makes sense on its own (the 'sea of distress' the exiles pass through), and the Greek can be explained as a different reading of the same letters (yam tsar, 'narrow sea,' for yam tsarah). Both fit the Exodus echo. The Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: The scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g) starts this verse in a gap: the printout shows only the word 'waves' and what follows, with 'in the sea' restored, so it does not preserve the phrase. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: they will go about in his name
t: Walk about, or boast, in his name?
p: The Hebrew says 'walk about'; the Greek has 'boast,' which one letter would change.

readings.plain: they will go about in his name
they will boast in his name

why: 'Walk about in his name' is an unusual phrase but fits Micah 4:5 ('we will walk in the name of the LORD our God'). 'Boast' is a very small change in Hebrew letters (a lamed for a kaf) and matches Psalm 105:3 and 1 Chronicles 16:10 ('boast in his holy name'). The Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: The scroll 4Q82 has this word in brackets, so the editors restore it (they read yithallelu, 'they will boast'); a restored word does not count as a reading of the scroll, and it is not cited here.

a: the forest no one could enter
t: The forest of the vintage, or the forest no one could enter?
p: The written text and the margin of the Masoretic Text differ by one letter.

readings.w: Margin (Qere) of the Masoretic Text; Septuagint 'the dense forest'
readings.plain: the forest no one could enter

readings.w: Written text (Ketiv) of the Masoretic Text

why: The margin (habbatsur, 'fortified, inaccessible') fits the poem: oaks of Bashan and a forest too thick to enter fall. 'The vintage forest' makes no sense next to cedar and oak. The Septuagint 'the dense forest' agrees with the margin.
b: 4Q82 breaks off just before this word. The King James Version has 'the forest of the vintage' (the written form).

t: The poor of the flock, or the Canaanite land?
p: The Hebrew word can be read 'poor'; the Greek reads the same letters as 'Canaanite.'

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text), probably reading the consonants as lik'na'ani
readings.orig: καὶ ποιμανῶ τὰ πρόβατα τῆς σφαγῆς εἰς τὴν Χαναανῖτιν
readings.en: and I will shepherd the flock for slaughter into the Canaanite land
readings.plain: I shepherded the flock meant for killing, in the land of Canaan

why: 'The poor of the flock' fits 9:9 (the same word) and 11:11. The Greek read the consonants of lakhen 'aniyye as lik'na'ani, a Canaanite, and made it a land or people. The Hebrew word kena'ani also means 'trader' (as in 14:21), which would bring in the sheep dealers of 11:5, but the Greek itself says 'Canaanite land,' not 'traders.' The Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: The Hebrew begins with lakhen, 'therefore,' a particle the Plain absorbs into 'So I shepherded.' The Greek has no 'therefore' because it read those letters differently. See also 11:11, where the Septuagint again has 'Canaanites.'

t: The poor of the flock, or the Canaanites?
p: As in 11:7, the Greek has 'Canaanites' where the Hebrew has 'the poor.'

readings.orig: γνώσονται οἱ Χαναναῖοι τὰ πρόβατα τὰ φυλασσόμενά μοι
readings.en: the Canaanites will know the sheep that are kept for me
readings.plain: the Canaanites will know the sheep kept for me

why: Same reasoning as 11:7: the Hebrew reading matches the earlier use of the phrase and gives a good sense (the humble sheep know that it is the word of the LORD). The Greek makes the Canaanites the ones who will know the sheep that are being kept for the LORD, probably reading the same letters as kena'ani; it does not say they tend the sheep. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

t: The potter or the treasury?
p: One letter separates 'potter' (yotser) from 'treasury' (otsar); the Greek has 'furnace.'

readings.w: A one-letter change in the Hebrew consonants (no manuscript named here)

why: The Hebrew has 'potter' and is the only form in any Hebrew manuscript. 'Treasury' is easier (the house of the LORD had a treasury, and 2 Kings 12:4-16 shows money paid into it) and is a one-letter change; the Greek 'furnace' may read yotser as 'a caster of metal.' But 'potter' is the harder reading, and Matthew 27:7, 10 (the Potter's Field) shows that a potter stood in the tradition Matthew knew. The Plain follows the Hebrew; see the note on Matthew's quotation.
b: The same word recurs in the last words of the verse ('to the potter'). The Septuagint reads 'furnace' both times. Matthew 27:6 says the priests would not put the money 'in the Temple treasury,' which has led some to think Matthew knew the reading 'treasury' and played on it.

t: The young one, or the scattered one?
p: The Greek has 'the scattered' where the Hebrew has na'ar, 'young.'
why: The Hebrew list is hard in any case. 'The young one' is unusual beside the perishing, broken and healthy sheep; the Greek 'scattered' makes a neat list and may read hanniddach. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

t: A bowl or a threshold?
p: The Hebrew word saf can mean either; the Greek chose 'threshold.'
why: Saf is a basin or bowl (Exodus 12:22, a basin for blood) and also a threshold or doorsill (Judges 19:27, 1 Kings 14:17). With ra'al, 'reeling,' the picture of a cup (Isaiah 51:17) is the better fit and matches the 'stone' of the next verse. The Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: 4Q82 preserves this verse in part and has saf ra'al; the printout shows the same consonants as the Masoretic Text for these words, so the scroll agrees with the Plain's reading.

t: Pierced, or mocked?
p: The Greek has 'because they danced in scorn'; John 19:37 has 'pierced.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 use the Greek verb for 'pierce'
readings.en: the one whom they pierced through
because they danced in triumph over (mocked)

why: The Septuagint translator probably read the Hebrew letters of daqaru (pierced) in another order, raqedu (danced), and gave 'danced against, mocked.' The Hebrew 'pierced' is the reading of the Masoretic Text, and John 19:37 has 'pierced' too. Rashi and the Targum take the Hebrew verb differently again; see the note on Jewish readings. The Plain follows the Hebrew. Whether the piercing is real or figurative, and who the pierced one is, is argued in the note.
b: The scroll 4Q80 has the word daqaru in brackets: restored, so it does not testify to this reading. In the same verse the scroll has 'to me' (elay) in clear letters.

a: the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo
t: Hadad-rimmon, or a pomegranate grove cut down?
p: The Greek does not read a name; it takes Rimmon as 'pomegranate.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4Q80 has 'Hadad' visible and 'Rimmon' and 'Megiddo' restored
readings.en: like the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo
readings.plain: the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo

readings.en: the mourning of a pomegranate grove in a plain being cut down
readings.plain: the mourning for a pomegranate grove cut down in the plain

why: The Greek understood rimmon as 'pomegranate' and found a verb in the rest; it gives a picture instead of a name, probably because the translator did not know the mourning referred to. The Hebrew names a mourning the readers knew. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: a man has owned me since I was young
t: Who owned the man, and what does he say?
p: The Hebrew verb is rare; the Greek reads 'a man fathered me.'

readings.en: a man has acquired me since my youth
readings.plain: a man has owned me since I was young

readings.orig: ἄνθρωπος ἐγέννησέν με ἐκ νεότητός μου
readings.en: a man begot me from my youth
readings.plain: a man fathered me when I was young

readings.w: A conjecture proposed by some modern commentators (not attributed to one here)
readings.en: the ground has owned me since my youth
readings.plain: the ground has been mine since I was young

why: The Hebrew hiqnani is a Hiphil of qanah ('acquire'), 'made me a possession,' a form that needs a note: he is owned like a slave or has been bought as a laborer. The Greek takes it as 'fathered,' the conjecture changes one letter to say 'the ground has been my possession.' The Plain follows the Hebrew, which says he is someone's property.

a: Strike the shepherd, and let the sheep be scattered
t: Strike the shepherd, or the shepherds?
p: The Hebrew has one shepherd and a command; the Greek has two plurals; Matthew has 'I will strike.'

readings.en: strike the shepherd, and let the sheep be scattered
readings.plain: Strike the shepherd, and let the sheep be scattered

readings.orig: πατάξατε τοὺς ποιμένας καὶ ἐκσπάσατε τὰ πρόβατα
readings.en: strike the shepherds, and draw out the sheep
readings.plain: Strike the shepherds, and pull the sheep away

why: The Hebrew is one imperative and a second verb (utefutsenah, 'and let them be scattered'). The Greek plural imperatives make the command general. The Hebrew is the older and harder reading, and the Plain follows it. Matthew 26:31 and Mark 14:27 use the first person, 'I will strike the shepherd,' which follows neither.
b: The printout shows no Qumran scroll for this verse. The Greek plural begins in the first colon: 'Sword, wake up against my shepherds and against a man, a citizen of mine' (epi tous poimenas mou), where the Hebrew has 'my shepherd.'

t: Raped, or lain with?
p: The written text has the harsh verb; the reader's margin has a gentler one.

readings.w: Written text (Ketiv) of the Masoretic Text, as the notes of the printout record
Margin (Qere), the form in the Leningrad text

why: The Jewish reading tradition replaced shagal with the milder shakhav in every place that has it (Deuteronomy 28:30; Isaiah 13:16; Jeremiah 3:2; here). In a conquest scene both words mean sexual violence, so the Plain says what the writer means. The Septuagint 'defiled' is a softer rendering of the same fact.

a: You will flee by the valley of my mountains
t: You will flee, or it will be blocked?
p: The same consonants can be read 'you will flee' or 'it will be blocked up.'

readings.en: and you will flee by the valley of my mountains
readings.plain: You will flee by the valley of my mountains

readings.orig: καὶ φραχθήσεται ἡ φάραγξ ὀρέων μου
readings.en: and the valley of my mountains will be blocked
readings.plain: The valley of my mountains will be blocked

why: The consonants wnstm can be pointed venastem ('and you will flee') or venistam ('and it will be stopped up'). The Septuagint reads the second and makes the new valley a closed one. The Hebrew reading gives an escape route and matches the second 'you fled' of the same verse. The Plain follows it.

t: With you, or with him?
p: The Hebrew speaks to 'you'; the Greek has 'with him.'
why: The Hebrew is the harder reading, since the speaker has just said 'the LORD my God will come,' and 'with you' turns to address the prophet or the people. 'With him' is the smoother form and is read by the Greek and many modern translators. The Plain follows the Hebrew; the sense is the same either way: the holy ones come with the LORD.

t: Cold and frost, or 'the bright ones will thicken'?
p: The written text and the margin differ; the whole line is among the hardest in the book.

readings.w: Margin (Qere) of the Masoretic Text; Septuagint 'cold and frost'
Written text (Ketiv) of the Masoretic Text
readings.plain: the bright ones will grow thick

why: Yeqarot can mean 'precious things' (the bright lights of the sky); the margin and the Septuagint take it as 'cold' (from qar). With the margin's 'and frost,' the line says: no light, but cold and frost. The written text instead says 'the bright ones will thicken (congeal).' Another common reading is 'no light, no cold or frost,' which needs a different word division. The Plain follows the margin and the Septuagint, which agree.

t: At Jerusalem, or against it?
p: The same Hebrew preposition can mean 'in' or 'against.'

readings.w: The same Hebrew, read with 'against' (as in some English versions, for example the NRSV)

why: This is one text read two ways, not two manuscripts. The Septuagint has 'in Jerusalem.' The note on this verse sets out why the Plain takes Judah on Jerusalem's side; 12:2 is the passage that favors 'against.'

a: no rain will fall on them
t: No rain, or 'these will be added to those'?
p: The Hebrew ends with the threat of no rain; the Greek has no rain at all.

readings.en: and not on them will be the rain
readings.plain: no rain will fall on them

readings.en: and these will be added to those
readings.plain: and these will be added to those

why: The Hebrew names the penalty of no rain, which is a real threat to Judah's farm country (see 10:1). The Greek has no rain and says only that those who do not go up 'will be added to those,' which seems to join them to the enemies of 14:12-15, or to those already punished; it may reflect a different Hebrew line or a free rendering. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: no rain will fall on them. The plague will strike them
t: No rain and a plague, or the plague only?
p: The Hebrew has an extra 'not'; the Greek leaves it out.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4Q76 (4QXII-a) has the 'and not' visible
readings.en: and not on them [rain]; there will be the plague
readings.plain: no rain will fall on them. The plague will strike them

readings.en: on these will be the plague

why: The Hebrew 'and not on them' has nothing to attach to; most read it as 'there will be no rain on them' continuing 14:17 (the Plain, which supplies the word 'rain' from 14:17), others as irony, since Egypt lives off the Nile, or as a copyist's addition. The Greek has no 'not' and makes it a plain threat of plague. The Plain follows the Hebrew, as 4Q76 supports.
b: The Qumran scroll 4Q76 (4QXII-a) has the end of the verse. The printout shows the second 'and not' in clear letters before the restored 'on them,' so the scroll agrees with the Masoretic Text on the extra 'not.' This is the only variant in the part with a clearly readable scroll against the Greek.

t: A Canaanite, or a trader?
p: The Hebrew says 'Canaanite'; the Aramaic Targum reads 'merchant.'

readings.w: Aramaic Targum of the Prophets (Targum Jonathan, an interpretive rendering; Aramaic text read on Sefaria)

why: 'Canaanite' is the word in all the Hebrew and Greek witnesses. It is also the Hebrew word for 'trader' (Proverbs 31:24; Zephaniah 1:11; Hosea 12:7), because the Canaanites (Phoenicians) were the great merchants. The Targum spells out the second sense. The Plain keeps 'Canaanite' and explains it in the note on the Temple.
